entries.title: What is Codex? How it differs from ChatGPT
entries.outcome: Codex is a coding agent that can inspect a project, edit files and run tools in a chosen environment. A model supplies its reasoning; a task is one assignment; a project groups related work and files. Unlike copying a code answer from chat into an editor, an agent can make the change in the workspace you selected.

entries.title: Accounts, sign-in, plans and usage
entries.outcome: Check how you signed in before interpreting usage. ChatGPT sign-in uses the Codex allowance associated with that account; API-key authentication in a supported client requires checking API billing separately. This tutorial teaches you where to verify your own allowance rather than freezing a price or message limit that may change.

entries.title: Choosing a Codex platform
entries.outcome: Compare desktop, mobile, CLI, IDE and cloud scenarios, and identify where files and tools run.

entries.title: Terminal paths and project roots
entries.outcome: Create a practice folder on Windows, macOS or Linux and distinguish current, relative and absolute paths.

entries.title: Finish your first small project
entries.outcome: Use an independent copy of the Small Steps todo website to change its heading and background. Identify the five practice files and compare the diff, core tests and two viewport widths while preserving behavior and data.

entries.title: Write a clear task request
entries.outcome: A useful request explains the outcome, available context, boundaries and acceptance checks. 'Improve the page' could mean speed, appearance or accessibility. Convert it into observable behavior before adding more instructions.

entries.title: Install and start Codex CLI
entries.outcome: Choose an installation platform, sign in, inspect a file, make a one-line change, verify it independently and resume the session. Includes a repeatable two-file exercise and a missing-file test.

entries.title: Windows CLI setup and troubleshooting
entries.outcome: Install and sign in from PowerShell, check command discovery, read a project and troubleshoot updates.

entries.title: macOS CLI setup and troubleshooting
entries.outcome: Set up the CLI in macOS Terminal and separate shell, update, directory and permission problems.

entries.title: Linux and WSL CLI environments
entries.outcome: Distinguish host and WSL tools, paths and accounts, then run the exercise and update from the right environment.

entries.title: Desktop: Windows, macOS and Linux
entries.outcome: The desktop workspace combines tasks, files, terminals and change review. Current official downloads use the name ChatGPT desktop app; choose Codex inside it. Follow the separate installation path for your system. Linux is a preview with a specific support list, not a promise of compatibility with every distribution.

entries.title: Get started in your IDE
entries.outcome: IDE integration places Codex beside your code for focused explanation and edits. VS Code, Cursor and Windsurf use the Codex extension; Xcode and JetBrains expose their own integration flows. Do not interchange their installation steps.

entries.title: Mobile: iPhone and Android
entries.outcome: Remote in the ChatGPT mobile app lets you guide Codex work on a connected computer. Official documentation lists iOS and Android clients, with Mac or Windows hosts, subject to rollout. This does not install a full development environment on the phone, and does not establish Linux host support.

entries.title: Continuing Codex work on iPhone or iPad
entries.outcome: Check the available iOS entry point, pairing and authentication, then track a supported task on its host.

entries.title: Continuing Codex work on Android
entries.outcome: Check the Android app, pairing and notifications, select the correct host and verify the task output.

entries.title: Remote setup, diagnosis and disconnection
entries.outcome: Pair devices, diagnose host availability and verify fresh file reads. Distinguish remote access, device pairing and task execution when stopping work.

entries.title: Cloud tasks and GitHub
entries.outcome: Cloud tasks run in a remote environment configured for a repository. They suit longer delegated work, but cannot automatically see uncommitted files on your computer. Creating a pull request is distinct from merging or deploying it.

entries.title: Cross-device handoff: files and environments
entries.outcome: Track the conversation, host, directory and branch so a handoff continues the intended work.

entries.title: Markdown and MD files
entries.outcome: Markdown uses plain-text markers for headings, lists, links and code, commonly in .md files. README.md explains a project, AGENTS.md supplies agent instructions and SKILL.md defines a reusable skill. An arbitrary MD file is not automatically an instruction source.

entries.title: Project instructions with AGENTS.md
entries.outcome: AGENTS.md supplies project instructions before Codex starts work. Global guidance and files along the project-root-to-working-directory path form an instruction chain. At the same level, AGENTS.override.md takes precedence. Keep rules concrete and verify what was actually loaded.

entries.title: AGENTS.md scopes and overrides
entries.outcome: Trace root and nested instructions, conflicts and overrides, and verify which files were selected.

entries.title: Separating rules, documentation and context
entries.outcome: Place project rules, usage instructions, design decisions and reusable workflows in suitable files.

entries.title: Configure Codex with config.toml
entries.outcome: config.toml sets client options, while AGENTS.md describes working instructions. User settings live in Codex home; trusted projects can add .codex/config.toml. CLI overrides, project layers and managed requirements mean a single file does not prove the effective configuration.

entries.title: Configuration precedence and diagnosis
entries.outcome: Trace ineffective or conflicting settings, change one item at a time and keep a reversible record.

entries.title: CLI commands and slash commands
entries.outcome: Distinguish shell commands and launch flags, interactive slash commands, keyboard shortcuts and natural-language requests. Check the input location: /plan belongs in the Codex interactive client; codex --help runs in the operating-system terminal.

entries.title: Sessions, resuming and forking
entries.outcome: Distinguish new, resumed and forked tasks, locate the right history and verify the directory and remaining work.

entries.title: Context and task handoff
entries.outcome: Long work needs durable decisions and evidence, not just a long conversation. README explains use, design documents explain choices, handoffs record current progress and AGENTS.md holds ongoing instructions. Do not turn all temporary progress into permanent rules.

entries.title: Choose a model, effort and speed
entries.outcome: Model choice affects available capabilities and usage conditions; reasoning effort affects how much work the agent devotes to a problem. Compare quality on the same small task before increasing effort. Use the options currently exposed by your account rather than assuming a named model is universally available.

entries.title: Plan mode: agree on the work first
entries.outcome: Plan mode is useful when scope or approach still needs decisions. It produces an implementation plan, not finished code. Define the questions to resolve and check that the plan includes inputs, outputs, constraints and verification.

entries.title: Permissions, sandbox, network and keys
entries.outcome: Sandbox rules define technical access to files and networks; approval policy determines when the agent asks before acting. No prompt does not guarantee permission, and read access does not imply write access everywhere.

entries.title: Manage desktop tasks and projects
entries.outcome: Keep follow-ups about one outcome in the same task and separate independent outcomes into different tasks. Projects identify files; tasks track assignments. Multiple tasks do not automatically isolate files: use worktrees when isolation is needed.

entries.title: Understanding an existing codebase
entries.outcome: Use a read-only workflow to locate entry points, data flow and tests, with file-backed explanations.

entries.title: Implementing the todo filters
entries.outcome: Implement Active and Completed filters from start, preserving data and verifying normal and boundary cases.

entries.title: A complete debugging workflow
entries.outcome: Debugging starts with a reproducible symptom, narrows causes with evidence and verifies the fix. Give the input, exact step, expected behavior and observed failure instead of only saying the site is broken.

entries.title: Git, branches, diffs and recovery
entries.outcome: Git stores file history, branches organize changes and diffs show what changed. Codex can help, but you must verify that the changes belong to the task. Restoring an old conversation does not restore Git files.

entries.title: Tests, code review and pull requests
entries.outcome: Tests check behavior under specified conditions, review examines the change for defects and a PR presents proposed integration. They complement each other: tests passing does not establish review approval, and an open PR is not a merge.

entries.title: Skills and SKILL.md
entries.outcome: A skill packages a repeatable workflow with instructions and optional resources. The minimum is a directory containing SKILL.md with name and description metadata followed by the procedure and expected output. Installation alone does not prove a task used it.

entries.title: Skill scripts, references and assets
entries.outcome: Move repeated logic and large references into useful resources, then verify conditional loading and relative paths.

entries.title: Testing skill selection and results
entries.outcome: Test format, selection and outcomes separately, using matching and non-matching requests to refine descriptions.

entries.title: Plugins and connected services
entries.outcome: A plugin can distribute skills and MCP tools as an installable capability. Installing it, connecting an external account and successfully calling a tool are distinct stages. A listing does not establish access to your data.

entries.title: Troubleshooting plugin connections
entries.outcome: Distinguish installation, account connection, authorization and callable tools before reconnecting or removing a plugin.

entries.title: Prompt, rules and handoff templates
entries.outcome: Choose a prompt, rule or handoff template, fill its required fields and use the correct input location.

entries.title: MCP setup and connection checks
entries.outcome: MCP connects Codex to tools and data. STDIO servers usually start as local processes; HTTP servers use a URL. Saving configuration only proves it exists: verify startup, authentication and an actual tool response.

entries.title: MCP connection diagnosis and recovery
entries.outcome: Inspect process, transport, authentication and tool discovery, preserve errors and verify a minimal operation.

entries.title: Worktrees and isolated tasks
entries.outcome: A Git worktree gives one repository multiple working directories on different branches. It isolates file edits, but databases, ports and external services may still be shared. File isolation is not full resource isolation.

entries.title: Subagents and task delegation
entries.outcome: Subagents suit independent work that can be reviewed and combined by the main task. They consume additional model and tool usage. Parallel tasks with mutual dependencies or overlapping edits can create more conflict than speed.

entries.title: Subagent scope and quality checks
entries.outcome: Define independent inputs, edit scopes and evidence, then review subagent results and resolve gaps.

entries.title: Integrating parallel work
entries.outcome: Integrate independent edits using file and interface contracts, resolve conflicts and verify combined behavior.

entries.title: Work with browsers, screenshots and images
entries.outcome: Visual work needs a reference, the actual result and explicit change criteria. Browser inspection, screenshots and generated concepts provide different evidence. A generated interface is not proof that a workflow works.

entries.title: Scheduled tasks and reminders
entries.outcome: Scheduled work needs a defined execution environment. A desktop task that reads local files requires the computer and app to be available at run time. Cloud work cannot directly read local data you have not supplied.

entries.title: codex exec and scripts
entries.outcome: codex exec runs one non-interactive task for scripts or CI. Normally progress goes to stderr and the final answer to stdout. --json produces JSON Lines events, not a single JSON object.

entries.title: JSON output and result validation
entries.outcome: Separate event streams from final results, parse structured output and reject missing or invalid fields.

entries.title: Codex in CI workflows
entries.outcome: Design a CI job with explicit input, permissions and exit states, preserving artifacts and separating proposals from application.

entries.title: Automation failure, retry and stopping
entries.outcome: Use execution records to detect prior effects, avoid duplicates, repair prerequisites and confirm a schedule has stopped.

entries.title: Workshop: build a small website
entries.outcome: This workshop connects clear requests, planning, MD instructions, browser checks and delivery. Build a fictional studio site with three cards in one HTML file. Practice a complete, inspectable result before expanding features.

entries.title: Workshop: build a CSV cleanup tool
entries.outcome: Build a CSV cleaner that preserves its input and writes a new output. The exercise trims whitespace, lowercases email, keeps the first occurrence of an address and skips blank names or malformed addresses. It reports kept, duplicate and invalid counts. Its format check does not prove a mailbox exists.

entries.title: Workshop: maintaining an existing project
entries.outcome: Establish a baseline, implement one change and deliver traceable regression checks and handoff notes.

entries.title: Project data, credentials and practice isolation
entries.outcome: Create fictional test data and restorable copies, and identify information to exclude from prompts, screenshots and repositories.

entries.title: Usage and efficiency: reducing rework
entries.outcome: Record task conditions, model options, time and outcomes to reduce unnecessary retries and excess context.

entries.title: Troubleshooting for beginners
entries.outcome: Start by locating the failing layer. A missing executable suggests installation or PATH; a rejected account suggests authentication; missing files suggest location or permissions; an incorrect result may involve the request or project code. Change one condition at a time.
